newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil re-election bill faces 2nd lower house vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil re-election bill faces 2nd lower house vote.

text.p: A constitutional amendment allowing Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election next year was due to be put to a second vote in the Chamber of Deputies later Tuesday, officials said.
Government whips were confident they would have little difficulty mustering the 308 votes needed for approval of the amendment. That amount of votes is equivalent to a three-fifths majority,
"It will be a peaceful vote," Deputy Jose Anibal, lower house whip with Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB) was quoted as saying newspapers.
The bill was approved for a first time in the lower house in January but needs a second vote before going to the Senate.
"The leaders think they have somewhere between 30 and 35 more votes than the 336 who voted for re-election in the first round," said a government official in Congress who asked not to be identified.

The first round of voting took place amid high tension in Congress after an anti-Cardoso wing of the normally government-allied Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) threatened to boycott the vote.
However, the election of the PMDB's Deputy Michel Temer as lower house president has since reduced resistance to re-election within the party.
Government whips were due to meet at midday to count how many deputies were in Brasilia to ensure quorum for today's session, due to begin at 1600 local/1900 GMT.
If the number was low, the re-election vote could be delayed until Wednesday, the government official said.
The government wants re-election approved quickly so it can hold a first lower house vote on its civil service reform bill, which seeks to cut jobs and costs in the public sector, he said.
That first vote could take place as early as next week. The government wants to get civil service reform through its two votes in the Chamber of Deputies by the end of March.
There are other factors behind the government's urgency to get re-election into the Senate.

Officials say they want to see progress on the amendment in the upper house before a revamped version of the governent's controversial social security reform bill is presented to the floor of the Senate, probably in about two months time.
Some observers also say the government expects there to be fallout from an ongoing inquiry in the Senate into alleged fraud involving state and municipal bonds.
"So the government wants re-election voted as soon as possible so one thing does not interfere with the other," Folha de Sao Paulo columnist Fernando Rodrigues said.

While most senators are in favor of re-election -- a poll late last year put support at 70 percent -- some are believed to want to rewrite the bill to force mayors and state governors to stand down during re-election campaigns.
That change, which would help the senators' own electoral ambitions, would send the amendment back to the Chamber of Deputies and will be opposed by the government.
